title: Prefrontal Cortical Activation Patterns and Cognitive Load Modulation in Adolescents: An 8-Channel EEG Analysis Across Task Domains, Procedural Familiarity, and Executive Network Recruitment
content: Adolescence is a period of major prefrontal development, yet little is known about how everyday activities engage the teenage prefrontal cortex. Eight-channel frontal EEG data were recorded (Neuroelectrics Enobio; FP1, FPZ, FP2, AF7, AF3, AF4, AF8, Fz; 500 Hz) from 20 recruited volunteers. Ten adolescents (ages 13 to 17) completed artifact-free recordings across 12 conditions: pre- and post-test resting baselines and ten 10-minute tasks (musical instrument, math problems, essay critique, Duolingo, chess puzzles, word puzzles, Rubik's cube, jigsaw puzzle, video games, and social media browsing). Signals were band-pass filtered (0.5 to 30 Hz), cleaned with independent component analysis, and average-referenced across channels using Python (SciPy and MNE-Python). Playing a musical instrument showed higher relative amplitude at AF3/AF7 than the resting baseline (t(9) = 2.86, p = 0.019, d = 0.90), and math problem solving did so at Fz (t(9) = 4.12, p = 0.0026, d = 1.30). Rubik's cube solving showed lower amplitude at AF7/Fz than the analytical tasks (t(9) = -3.41, p = 0.0077, d = 1.08), consistent with the neural efficiency hypothesis that practiced skills demand less prefrontal effort. These findings are exploratory: the sample was small, the measure was broadband and average-referenced, and muscle artifact could not be fully excluded. The report discusses each limitation and proposes follow-up designs.
